[3] (7) Forbidden for benefit. For the sages penalized him since he transgressed bal yera'eh and bal yimatzei [Gemara].
[3] (8) He left it inadvertently. Meaning that he did not know about that chametz.
[3] (9) Or under unavoidable circumstances. This means that he knew about it but was under unavoidable circumstances and could not destroy it. Even though in this case he did not transgress bal yera'eh, nevertheless we penalize permitted cases because of prohibited ones, for if we permit it to him, he may come to leave it intentionally ab initio and transgress regarding it. See Biur Halacha. Beis Hillel in Yoreh De'ah, siman 132, wrote: I was asked about a Jew who before Pesach had grain at a non-Jew's mill to grind, and the grain was delayed at the mill until Chol HaMoed of Pesach. When the seventh day of Pesach came, the non-Jew went and ground the Jew's grain, made bread from the flour, baked the bread, and brought the bread to the Jew immediately after Pesach. I answered that it is permitted to take payment for that bread from the non-Jew, and that non-Jew should eat it or sell it to a non-Jew; see there. Chok Yaakov agreed that it is permitted even for eating, because perhaps the non-Jew exchanged the grain, so it is only doubtful chametz that remained over Pesach (see below, siman 449). Beis Meir inclines to permit eating it for another reason: although the Mechaber ruled that whether inadvertent or unavoidable it is forbidden, not all unavoidable circumstances are equal. In such an unavoidable case, where he could not at all have considered that the non-Jew would bake his flour into chametz, the sages certainly did not penalize him; see there. See in Biur Halacha what I wrote in the name of Radbaz. If a Jew left wheat in a mill and a non-Jew came and told the Jew that he had soaked and ground it, see Chok Yaakov in the name of Chinuch Beis Yehudah, that there are many doubts here for leniency. Pri Megadim questions this where it is the practice of the local people to soak wheat before grinding, and he inclines that the non-Jew should exchange it for other wheat.
[3] (10) And if he sold it, etc. Which modes of acquisition a non-Jew uses to acquire will be written below at the end of the se'if.
[3] (11) To a non-Jew. It is forbidden to sell to an apostate Jew, for his law is like that of a Jew in every respect, and one also transgresses lifnei iver; the chametz is forbidden for benefit after Pesach. After the fact, if he sold to an apostate Jew for a small amount because he recognizes him and knows that he will return it to him after Pesach, since he erred and thought that an apostate's law is like that of a non-Jew, in a case of great loss one may permit him to tell the apostate to exchange the chametz with a non-Jew for other chametz, or to sell it, and those exchanged items or the money will be permitted, as explained at the end of siman 443.
[3] (12) Outside the house. The later authorities wrote that there is no concern about the non-Jew himself, whether he lives in his house or not. Rather, the main concern is that the non-Jew remove the chametz from the Jew's house. As for the non-Jew himself, even if he is the Jew's servant and lives in his house, we have no concern (unless he is permanently acquired by him, for then his hand is like his master's hand, and selling to him is ineffective, since the item has not left his domain through this). As to why they required here that the chametz be removed from his domain, although he has already sold it and it is merely with him as a deposit without responsibility, and in general in such a case we require only a partition, as above in siman 440, Chok Yaakov wrote that here too the law is so. They required here that he remove it from his domain only so that the non-Jew acquire the chametz by pulling; and indeed, if the non-Jew already removed the chametz and acquired it by pulling to his house or to a side alley according to law, he may afterward bring the chametz into the Jew's house, and a partition of ten handbreadths alone is enough. But several later authorities wrote that here it is worse, for since the non-Jew knows that the main chametz belongs to the Jew and will not touch it, even though he acquired it, if it remains in the Jew's house it appears like the Jew's chametz. There is also concern that he may come to eat it, because since it was originally his, he does not keep away from it. According to this view, even if he designated a separate corner in his house or made a partition of ten handbreadths, it also does not help. All this, however, is only ab initio. After the fact, it is obvious that one should not forbid it at all, and even if he did not designate a place for it, as long as the sale was according to law. The later authorities wrote that if he has much chametz and it is impossible to remove it from his house, he should also sell him the room, and it is like selling it to him outside his house. Acquisition of the room is by money together with a document. If he fears giving him a document lest he decide to take possession of the chametz, and there is great loss, he should stipulate with him that he acquire it with money alone without a document, and such a stipulation is effective according to several poskim; one may rely on this leniently in such a case. He must hand him the key to the room in which the chametz is located so that he can enter whenever he wants and take his chametz that was sold or given to him. Or at least the Jew should say to him: whenever you want, you can take the key to your room and enter it to take your chametz. It is an absolute prohibition to leave any seal or lock on the room or on the chametz so that the non-Jew cannot take the chametz, for this proves that the whole sale was merely evasion. If he did so from the outset, at the time he sold it, the chametz is forbidden even after the fact, because the non-Jew did not rely on the sale. Nevertheless, if at first he sold it according to law and afterward placed a lock on the room or a seal on the chametz, although it is forbidden to do so, the chametz is not forbidden because of what he did improperly after the sale. See Biur Halacha, where we wrote in the name of Pri Megadim and Chayei Adam distinctions in this law.
[3] (13) And he will go back and give it to him. If the non-Jew does not wish to return it to him, it is forbidden to sue him in their courts or compel him by other forms of compulsion. But if he gave him only part of the money and the rest was recorded as a loan, and he does not wish to pay the remainder, it is certainly permitted to sue him in their courts so that he pay what is owed, or give him the chametz as payment for his debt. The later authorities wrote that another Jew is forbidden to buy the chametz from the non-Jew after Pesach. If he bought it, he must return it to the original owners. If he paid the non-Jew more than what is proper to pay in such a case, the original owner need return to him only the amount that is proper to pay.
[3] (14) Provided that he give it, etc. Even through his agent or his wife he can transfer ownership of the chametz to the non-Jew, but not through a non-Jew, for there is no agency for a non-Jew, and his sale is nothing. Likewise, he cannot transfer it to the non-Jew's agent, because the Torah included agency only for a Jew. This is so even if the agent is also a non-Jew, for there is no agency for a non-Jew, whether from a non-Jew to a Jew or from a non-Jew to a non-Jew. See in Biur Halacha what I wrote in this regard in the name of several poskim.
[3] (15) A complete gift. Acquisition by gift is through lifting, or through pulling in the case of an item that cannot be lifted.
[3] (16) Without any condition. For perhaps the non-Jew will violate the condition, and the gift will be void retroactively, and he will have transgressed bal yera'eh, as below in se'if 4.
[3] (17) Or that he sell it to him. Regarding which acquisitions a non-Jew uses to acquire, there are different views among the poskim. Some say that a non-Jew's acquisition is specifically by money. Others say that a non-Jew acquires only through pulling into his domain, or by lifting an item that can be lifted. Others wrote further that other acquisitions also apply to a non-Jew, such as acquisition of movable goods together with land, acquisition through a courtyard, and exchange acquisition, meaning kinyan sudar. One must be careful with this that the sudar belong to the non-Jew, and it is not enough for the witnesses to the acquisition to give their sudar as with a Jew, because that works only by the principle of acquiring on behalf of the transferor, and regarding a non-Jew there is no law of acquiring on another's behalf. Some question these acquisitions and say that we find them only regarding a Jew. As a matter of law, ab initio he certainly must transfer it through a complete acquisition that is agreed upon by all, namely with money and pulling together, since this touches on the biblical prohibition of bal yera'eh. At the very least, pulling alone is sufficient, for through this he also fulfills the view of most poskim. But after the fact, even if he sold it only with money, or sold it with one of the other acquisitions we mentioned, and Pesach passed over it, it is permitted. Since chametz after Pesach is forbidden only because of a rabbinic penalty, and furthermore, since chametz after the time of its prohibition is in any case no longer in his domain, except that Scripture made it as though it were in his domain so that he transgresses regarding it, any acquisition is enough, for at least he reveals his intent that he does not want it and has removed it from his domain. In a place where it is impossible to transfer it by pulling, such as where there is much chametz or it is on the road, this will be explained below.
[3] (18) A complete sale. If a Jew leaves his chametz in the room of his fellow, who is selling his chametz, he must inform the Jewish seller and make him an agent to sell it. If he left it without his knowledge, it is forbidden after Pesach, since the Jew did not know to transfer ownership and the non-Jew did not know to acquire it [later authorities]. They wrote further that a person may say to a non-Jew: here is this chametz, and after Pesach you will give me other chametz.
[3] (19) For a small amount. There is no concern for voiding the sale because of underpricing, for he himself knows that it is worth more and agrees to transfer it to him so that it not remain in his domain and become forbidden for benefit. It is better for him to sell it to his acquaintances, because in that case presumably the non-Jew will return it to him after Pesach. See Biur Halacha regarding our present custom. The later authorities wrote that although ab initio one should sell with money and pulling, nevertheless, if there is much chametz and it is impossible to pull all the chametz, and likewise if the chametz is not here so that the non-Jew can pull it, but is in another city or on the road, he should transfer it to the non-Jew through other acquisitions, such as through a mark, where in some places the custom is that the buyer marks the acquired item so that he has a known sign on it, and through this he acquires it, or through a handshake, called "tzu shlag," meaning that they strike their palms against one another, or through giving a perutah in places where the custom is that when the buyer gives a perutah to the seller the sale is completed, or in a place where the custom is that handing over the key completes the sale. In any case, however, he must say, "I hereby sell you such-and-such chametz for such-and-such sum," unlike what the masses say, "I hereby sell you the key," for that is not considered anything. So too, anything like this, each place according to the merchants' custom, is considered an acquisition according to Torah law, and one may properly transfer the chametz through such an acquisition as well. Or he may sell the chametz through agav, meaning that he should sell the non-Jew land or a room, or rent it to him, and together with it say to him, "Acquire the chametz that I have in the place of the land, or wherever it is," for through agav he acquires even if the items are not piled there. The land is acquired by the non-Jew with money and a document, and for rental, money alone is enough. Even if the non-Jew does not give him all the money, but only a few coins, called "auf gab," that is enough, and the Jew should stipulate with him that with this auf gab he acquires the room and the chametz, while the rest of the money is recorded as a loan. They wrote further that if the house where the chametz is located is not his, but is rented by him, then his sale is ineffective, for how can he sell something that is not his? Rather, he should rent that room to the non-Jew, and rent it to him without specification, so that he may keep his vessels and movable goods there, and he should not explicitly say that he is renting it to place chametz inside it, as below in siman 450. A Jew who bought chametz from a non-Jew and gave money but has not yet pulled it: although ab initio he certainly should sell it before Pesach, for according to several poskim money acquires between a Jew and a non-Jew, nevertheless, if he did not sell it and Pesach passed over it, it is permitted, for according to most poskim he acquires only by pulling. But if he pulled it, even if he did not give money, and Pesach passed over it, one should forbid it. However, if according to the merchants' custom acquisition is made with money, Pri Megadim inclines to be stringent even in the first case; see Sha'arei Teshuvah, se'if katan 9.
[3] (20) On condition to return. Meaning after Pesach.
[3] (21) It is ineffective. Even though throughout the Torah a gift on condition to return is considered a gift if the condition is fulfilled, here the sages required a complete gift because of the stringency of chametz. Regarding after the fact, if the condition was fulfilled and he returned it, whether it is permitted is disputed by the later authorities; see Biur Halacha. Where he said, "I hereby give it to you and you will return it to me," see Biur Halacha.

peri_megadim.he:
וטוב עט״ז דיעבד אפילו שותק כל שלא עשה מעשה אמרינן דאיסורא לא ניחא דליקני אפילו משתמרת ועומד שם עב״י וע״ש:
והוי יודע דחצירו של אדם אם ניחא ליה קונה אף איסורי הנאה כבסי׳ תמ״ו ומ״ז כי מגביה ישראל קנאו. ומיהו סתם איסורי אכילה מסתמא לא מפקרי בעלים ועיין מהרש״א ז״ל ביצה ל״ח ב׳ דסתם אסורי אכילה בעלים מפקירין עמדתי בפריי לי״ד וצ״ע ומספקא לי איסורי הנאה אי סתמו הפקר או לאו ונ״מ בגר שיש פקדון אצל ישראל ומת קודם הלילה ואמר הישראל קודם שמת יזכה לי חצירו ומת ואח״כ חזר הישראל ואמר שאין רוצה לזכות בו קודם שמת הגר ולמ״ד כל דלא עבר כ״א בעשה תשביתו לא קנסו כדבעינן למימר באות ו׳ ז׳ ובמ״א ג׳ למ״ד דקנסו בעבר אע״ה יצוייר בשש דהשתא אי סתם איסורי הנאה ד״ת או דרבנן הפקר הם כבר זכה הישראל ומה שחזר אח״כ א״י דלאו ברשותו תו להפקיר ועבר ב״י ואסור לאחר הפסח משא״כ אי סתמו לאו הפקר לא זכה ישראל מעולם וכיון שחזר קודם שמת לאו של ישראל ומותר לאחר הפסח. סבור הייתי ללמוד זה מירושלמי פ״ט דשביעית ה״ה ר׳ חזקיה סליק גבי ר׳ ירמיה אמר ליה זכיתי לי אוצרי א״ל צור לי אילין פריטין גבך וא״ל הרי מקומך מושכר לי א״ל לא כן אפקרתן חזר וזכיתה בהן ופי׳ המפרש הגאון מהר״ר אליהו ז״ל דר״ח אמר דפירות שביעית בשעת הביעור רחמנא אפקריה וזכה בהן כו׳ ור״י אמר דשוכר מקומו ותקנה לו ואמר ר״ח לדידן דלא אפקרתן אסור כדין זמן הביעור יע״ש וזה יש לדחות:
peri_megadim.en:
[3] And it is good. See Taz. After the fact, even if he is silent, as long as he did no act, we say that he does not want to acquire a prohibition, even in a guarded courtyard and even if he is standing there. See Beis Yosef and see there.
[3] Know that a person's courtyard, if he wants it, acquires even items forbidden for benefit, as in siman 446 and Mishbetzos Zahav there, where when the Jew lifts it he acquires it. However, ordinary items forbidden for eating presumably are not made ownerless by their owners. See Maharsha, of blessed memory, Beitzah 38b, that ordinary items forbidden for eating are made ownerless by the owners. I discussed this in my Pri Megadim to Yoreh De'ah, and it requires examination. I am uncertain regarding items forbidden for benefit: are they presumptively ownerless or not? A practical difference is a convert who has a deposit by a Jew and dies before nightfall, and before the convert died the Jew said, "My courtyard should acquire it for me," and he died, and afterward the Jew retracted and said that he did not wish to acquire it before the convert died. According to the view that where he transgressed only the positive commandment of tashbisu they did not penalize him, as we will want to say in notes 6 and 7 and in Magen Avraham 3, and according to the view that they did penalize even for transgressing a positive commandment, the case can be drawn at the sixth hour. Now, if ordinary items forbidden for benefit, whether biblically or rabbinically, are ownerless, the Jew already acquired it, and his later retraction is ineffective, for it is no longer in his possession to make ownerless; he transgressed bal yera'eh, and it is forbidden after Pesach. But if they are not presumptively ownerless, the Jew never acquired it, and since he retracted before the convert died, it is not the Jew's and is permitted after Pesach. I thought to learn this from the Yerushalmi, chapter 9 of Shevi'is, halachah 5: R. Chizkiyah went up to R. Yirmiyah and said to him, "Acquire my stores for me." He said to him, "Keep these coins with you for me," and said to him, "Your place is rented to me." He said to him, "Did you not make them ownerless? You went back and acquired them." The Gaon, R. Eliyahu, of blessed memory, explained that R. Chizkiyah said that produce of shemittah at the time of bi'ur is made ownerless by the Merciful One, and he acquired it, etc.; R. Yirmiyah said that he rents his place and it acquires for him. R. Chizkiyah said: according to us, who did not make them ownerless, it is forbidden as under the law of the time of bi'ur; see there. But this can be rejected.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: <small>סעיף ג' </small>אם מכרו במה שכותבים בשטר מכירה לנכרי כל חמצי מכור לך הא להרמב"ם והמ"ע לחו"המ ססי' ר"ח לא מהני כיון דאינו מזכיר מין מסויים עמ"ש בתשובה:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [3] <small>Se'if 3.</small> If he sold it by means of what they write in the bill of sale to the non-Jew, "All my chametz is sold to you," according to the Rambam and the Maggid Mishneh to Choshen Mishpat, end of siman 208, this is ineffective, since he does not mention a specific type. See what I wrote in a responsum.

turei_zahav.he: וטוב שיאמר כו'. דמצד הדין אפי' בלא אמירה שרי דאמרי' דהתירא ניחא לי' דלקני רשות ולא איסורא:
turei_zahav.en: [3] And it is good that he say, etc. For by strict law, even without saying it, it is permitted, since we say that he wants his domain to acquire a permitted item, not a prohibited one.

mechaber.he: רשאי ישראל לומר לעכו"ם בשעה חמישית או קודם עד שאתה לוקח חמץ במנה קח במאתים שמא אצטרך ואקחנו ממך אחר הפסח אבל לא ימכור לו ולא יתן לו על תנאי ואם עשה כן הרי זה עובר בבל יראה ובל ימצא:
mechaber.en: A Jew is permitted to say to a non-Jew in the fifth hour or earlier: While you are acquiring chametz for one hundred [coins], acquire [it] for two hundred, as perhaps I will need [chametz] and I will buy it from you after Passover. But he may not sell it to him or give it to him on condition [that he will return it], and if he did so, he transgresses [the prohibitions of] 'it shall not be seen' and 'it shall not be found.

baer_heitev.he:
ואקחנו. ורשאי אפי' להבטיחו שיחזור ויקנה ממנו ושיתן לו ריוח. ב"ח ואחרונים:
ע"ת. נראה פירושו על תנאי שיחזירנו לו אחר פסח דא"כ לא הוי מכירה ולא מתנה אבל אם א"ל ע"ת שתחזיקהו לעצמך ותעשה בו כרצונך רק שלא תמכרם לשום אדם אחר דזה הוי מכירה גמורה. ט"ז ע"ש:
baer_heitev.en:
[4] And I will buy it. He is permitted even to promise that he will buy it back from him and will give him a profit. Bach and the later authorities.
[4] On condition. It appears that the meaning is: on condition that he return it to him after Pesach, for then it is neither a sale nor a gift. But if he said to him: on condition that you keep it for yourself and do with it as you wish, only that you not sell it to any other person, this is a complete sale. Taz; see there.

beer_hagolah.en:
(א) in the Tosafot mentioned

(ב) Rambam, chapter 4

beur_hagra.en:
[4] Se'if 4: he is permitted. This is from the Tosefta and Yerushalmi there.
[4] But not. As above.

chatam_sofer.he: <small>(שם במג"א סק"ד)</small> אבל עכו"ם לעכו"ם עושה. נ"ב עיין ש"ך חו"מ סי' רמ"ג סק"ה ובבית שמואל ס"ס ה':
chatam_sofer.en: [4] <small>There, in Magen Avraham, se'if katan 4.</small> "But a non-Jew can make another non-Jew an agent." Note: see Shach, Choshen Mishpat, siman 243, se'if katan 5, and Beis Shmuel, end of siman 5.

eliyah_rabbah.he: [ד] ביום אחרון וכו'. וכן משמע בראשון אלא דקא משמע לן דאף באחרון צריך שלא יהא ניכר, שאם קבלם אסור בהנאה ואם לא היה ניכר אף בראשון מותר. כתב חק יעקב אם באחרון אין צריך כפיית כלי ומחיצות עשרה אבל תוך הפסח צריך כפיית כלי או מחיצה עשרה, עד כאן, וזה סותר לכאורה מה שכתב בסימן ת"מ דצריך לבערו, ולדינא כתבתי בס"ק ח' דעיקר דאין צריך לבער רק אם הוא ביום טוב דאי אפשר לעשות מחיצה יכפה כלי ובחול המועד יעשה מחיצה, ובאחרון נראה נמי דיכפה כלי שהרי כתב שם אם לא הניחו אלא לחצי יום יכפה כלי, עד כאן, מיהו אם מביאו אחר מנחה ודאי אין צריך. וזה לשון צידה לדרך באחרון אין להראות למביאים שרוצה לקנותו אלא שיניחו הכותים בקרן זוית של הבית עד כאן לשונו:
eliyah_rabbah.en: [4] On the last day, etc. So too it is implied regarding the first day; rather, it teaches us that even on the last day it must not be recognizable, for if he accepted them they are forbidden for benefit, and if it was not recognizable, then even on the first day it is permitted. Chok Yaakov wrote: on the last day, covering with a vessel and a partition of ten handbreadths are not required, but during Pesach one needs covering with a vessel or a partition of ten handbreadths. This is the end of his words. This seemingly contradicts what he wrote in siman 440, that he must destroy it. As a matter of law, I wrote in se'if katan 8 that the main view is that he does not need to destroy it; rather, if it is on Yom Tov, when he cannot make a partition, he should cover it with a vessel, and on Chol HaMoed he should make a partition. On the last day too, it appears that he should cover it with a vessel, for he wrote there that if he left it only for half a day he should cover it with a vessel. This is the end of his words. However, if he brings it after minchah, he certainly need not do so. This is the language of Tzeidah LaDerech: on the last day, one should not show the bringers that he wants to acquire it; rather, the non-Jews should leave it in a corner of the house. This is his language.

eshel_avraham.he: עובר. כ' הפר"ח זה לסברת סי' ח"מ ע"ש שא"ז העיקר. וא"א ע"מ להחזיר אי ע"מ שתעשה דבר פלוני ה"ז מכירה גמורה. ועיין ח"מ סי' רי"ב ס"ב ובא"ע סימן כ"ח אך משו' חומרא דחמץ אסור ועיין ס"ג:
eshel_avraham.en: He transgresses. Pri Chadash wrote this per view of siman 440 (see there) that is the main point. Gift on condition to return — if on condition you do such-and-such, this is absolute sale. See Choshen Mishpat siman 212 seif 2 and Avnei Nezer siman 28; however because of chametz stringency forbidden; see seif 3.

levushei_serad.he: <small>(ש"ע)</small> או שימכרנו לו מכירה גמור' וכו' עיין שו"ת מ"ב סימן ז'
levushei_serad.en: [4] <small>Shulchan Aruch.</small> "Or that he sell it to him as a complete sale, etc." See Responsa M.B., siman 7.

machatzit_hashekel.he:
(ס"ק ד) שמחוץ כו' פי' גם החמץ משמע דהגוי וודאי צ"ל חוץ לבית ואסור למכרו לגוי הדר עמו וכ"ד הרב"י. אבל האחרונים חלקו דאין כוונת ת"ה כ"א על החמץ שיהיה חוץ לבית אבל בגוי לא איכפת לן אם לא שהוא עבדו כנעני דגופו קנוי לו ויד עבד בזה כיד רבו דמי:
ואם יש לו חמץ הרבה וא"א לו להוציא כו' משמע דוקא כה"ג דא"א לו להוציאו מותר אבל אם אפשר להוציאו מתוך הבית צריך להוציאו וכ"כ בספר א"ר שכן המנהג בפראג שמוכרי שכר צריכים להוציא כל החמץ מתוך ביתם ושאלוהו מה נשתנו הם ממוכרי יין שרף שהותר להם שיהי' החמץ בביתם וימכרוהו לגוי. והשיב להם דשאני מוכרי יי"ש שא"א להם להוציא החמץ ע"ש:
אלא עם השטר ר"ל בעי' תרתי כסף וגם שטר ואין קפידא אם נתן כסף תחלה או שטר תחלה כ"ה שם בח"מ וכ' בשל"ה דאפי' נכתב השטר בגופן שלנו דהיינו בכתב יהודית וז"ל שכותב לגוי חדר פלוני מכר עם כל מה שבתוכו עכ"ל ומ"ש עם כל כו' עמ"ש להבא:
והנה' כו' בכסף לחוד וסיים של"ה ע"ז מ"מ צריך לאודעי לגוי ולהבינו הדבר היטב כדי שיהיה דעתו סומכת לקלות עכ"ל:
ב"ח. באמת כאן כתב הב"ח דסגי אם מתנה שיקנה בכסף לחוד אולם שם בח"מ הביא ש"ך בשם הב"ח שחולק על דין זה וס"ל דלא מהני מה שמתנה לקנות בכסף גרידא ואפשר דגבי חמץ מקיל הב"ח כיון דבלא"ה אינו ברשותו אלא שעשאו הכתוב כאלו הוא ברשותו וכמ"ש מ"א אח"ז:
ועסי' ת"ן ס"ה ר"ל דהב"ח כתב אע"ג דאפשר שישכיר החדר לגוי שכירות קרקע גם לגוי נקנה ע"י כסף גרידא אלא דלא אפשר מתרי טעמא חדא דקי"ל שכירות לא קניא ועוד דאיתא בירושלמי דאין להשכיר חדר לגוים להשתמש בו חמץ והפר"ח דחה טעמים הנ"ל דמ"ש שכירות לא קניא הא מ"מ גבי חמץ מהני וכדאמרינן בפסחים דף ד' שאני חמץ דכתיב לא ימצא וגם ע"י שכירות אינו מצוי אצלו ומ"ש שהירושלמי אוסר הא לא קיי"ל כהאי ירושלמי ואעפ"כ לדינא הסכים עם הב"ח דאין תקנה ע"י שכירות דה"ל משתכר באיסורי הנאה דאסור ומה"ט כתב בסי' ת"ן סעיף ה' במ"א ס"ק וי"ו דאין להשכיר לגוי בערב פסח או תוך הפסח לשום בו חמץ וזהו כוונת מ"א ממה שרמז לעיין בסי' ת"נ ס"ה ומזה משמע דשאלה מותרת וכ"כ פר"ח שם וגם שאלה ניקנית בכסף גרידא וגם יכול לקנות ע"י זה גם חמץ:
ועיי' של"ה כבר הבאתיו לעיל:
והמ"ב כו' בכסף ובמשיכה כו'. דבר"פ הזהב פליגי ר"י ור"ל ר"י ס"ל ד"ת מעות קונה בישראל וכתב רחמנא וכי תמכרו ממכר לעמיתך וממעט גוי א"כ בגוי לא מהני קנין כסף אלא בעי' משיכה ור"ל ס"ל מן התורה בישראל משיכה קונה וא"כ בגוי הוי איפכא דוקא כסף קונה ולא משיכה ופסק רש"י והעומדים בשיטתו כר"ל ור"ת והעומדים בשיטתו פסקו כר"י ולצאת ידי שניהם כתב בי"ד סי' ש"ך לענין להפקיע קדושת בכור להקנות האם בעודה מעוברת לגוי ובהמת גוי פטורה מן הבכורה לקנין זה הצריך שם תרתי כסף ומשיכה או הקנאת מקום שעומדת הבהמה שם וע"ז קונה גם הפרה וה"ה הכא:
דרוב הפוסקים ס"ל כרש"י כצ"ל באמת כ' האחרונים דאדרבה רוב הפוסקים ס"ל כר"ת אלאדאין נ"מ לדינא דמ"מ מהני דיעבד. כסף לחוד דהא מ"ב כ' דגם משיכה לחוד מהני דיעבד. אע"ג דלדעתו רוב הפוסקים ס"ל דבעי' בגוים דוקא כסף א"כ ה"ה לדידן אפכא מהני דיעבד כסף לחוד אע"ג דרוב הפוסקים ס"ל כר"ת דבעי' בגוי משיכה. בגילוי דעתא סגי כמ"ש בב"י סי' תל"א דמה"ט מהני ביטול מתורת הפקר ולדעת כמה פוסקים אפי' ביטול בלב מהני אע"ג דכה"ג לא מהני גבי הפקר דהא לא אמר לשון הפקר אלא לבטל להוי כעפרא (גם לי"א בעינן דוקא הפקר בפני שלשה) וכמ"ש בח"מ סי' רע"ג סעיף ז':
וצ"ע דבירושלמי כו' דאין גוי ע"ש לגוי חבירו כו' הנה בענין הקנאות מקום נבוכו הרבה בס' ח"י כ' בשם תשובת א"ש דאין הכוונה שעי"ז שמקנה לו המקום ה"ל חצירו של גוי וקונה לו חצירו את החמץ דהא חצר מטעם שליחות אתרבאי ואין שליחות לגוי אע"כ הכוונה בתורת אגב דמטלטלין נקנית אגב קרקע (ולפ"ז צ"ל לשון אגב ולא לשון עם כמ"ש בח"מ סי' ר"ב לדעת י"א שם) ואולם בתשובת עבודת הגרשוני ס"ס ק"כ כ' דמה"ט כתב הטור י"ד סי' ש"ך לענין הפקעות קדושת בכור דהמחוור שבקנינים ש קנה לו המקו' ונתן בתשובה הנ"ל טעם למה קנין זה המחוור דבמשיכה אין דעת הגוי לקנות כ"א בכסף וכל היכי דאין דעת הקונ' לקנות לא מהני קנין ואייתי ראיה מדאמרינן בב"מ דף יו"ד נפל העני על הפיאה מעבירים אותו הימנה דלא קני ואע"ג דקיי"ל ד"א של אדם קונות לו מ"מ דכיון דנפל עליו גלי' דעתיה דבנפילה ניחא ליה למיקנא ולא בד"א ולכן אין הד"א קונות לו הרי דבדעת הקונה תליא הקנין וכ"כ הרב"י בסי' קל"ד וגם הב"ח שם וכ' שכ"כ בתשובת ר"מ מינץ והרבה בראיות לכן עדיף הקנאות מקום חצירו קונה לו שלא מדעתו עכת"ד. לפ"ז ע"כ ס"ל דהטעם בחצר קונה לגוי ולא מטעם אגב דא"כ אכתי בעינן דעת גוי ואדרבה קנין אגב קשה להבינו לגוי. וקרוב שאין דעת הגוי לקנות ע"י אגב אע"כ לדעת תשובת ע"ה הטעם מתורת חצר ותקשי' לדידיה קושית תשובת א"ש הנ"ל דהא אין שליחות לגוי ומצאתי שבתשו' ע"ה ס"ס ק"ה הרגיש בזה וכ' וז"ל גם י"ל במה שהגוי חצירו קונה לו הלא חצירו משום שליחות ואנן קיי"ל אין שליחות לגוי והארכתי בזה בתשובה אחרת עכ"ל. ואני לא מצאתי דאתי לידי בתשובותיו הנדפסות מזה דבר ואולי י"ל דס"ל כהמ"ב שמביא מ"א דגוי לגוי נעשה שליח כיון דשניהם אינן בני ברית דוקא כשהמשלח בן ברית גם השליח צ"ל בן ברית וה"ה איפכא כששליח ב"ב גם המשלח צ"ל ב"ב אבל בששניהם המשלח ושליח אינו ב"ב ש"ד. ולפ"ז אע"ג דחצר מטעם שליחות מ"מ חצר קונה לגוי דהא גם החצר לאו ב"ב ונעשה שליח לגוי. ובתשובת ח"ש אזיל לשיטתיה דלא ברירא ליה אי גוי לגוי נעשה שליח כמ"ש בס' ח"י משמו ולכן כתב שלא להקנות לגוי ע"י חצר כ"א בתורת אגב. וא"כ כיון שהוכיח מ"א מן הירושלמי דגוי לגוי אינו נעשה שליח א"כ קיי"ל כתשובת א"ש דאין חצר קונה לגוי וצריך להקנות לו החמץ מתורת אגב:
וכבר כתבתי דקשה להקנות לגוי ע"י אגב דאין דעת הגוי סומכת לקנות ע"י אגב והיכי דאין דעתו לקנות בקנין זה לא קנה כמ"ש בשם תשובת ע"ה בשם הפוסקים. ולכן עלה ברוחי דעדיף למכור לאשה גויה שאין לה בעל דכה"ג א"ל דמודה תשובת א"ש דחצרה קונה לה דמבואר בח"מ סי' רמ"ג דקטן אין לו חצר דלגבי איש חצר מטעם שליחות אתרבאי ואין שליחות לקטן אבל קטנה יש לה חצר דגבי אשה חצר משום יד אתרבאי וקטנה יש לה יד. ואם כן אשה גויה י"ל חצר דהא א"ל יד ואע"ג דהא דאתרבאי חצר באשה משום יד ילפינן מגט כדאיתא פ"ק דב"מ וגט ליתא בגוי מ"מ י"ל דכיון דלא נתמעט גוי מקנין זה גם באשת גויה הדין כן. תדע דהא קנין אגב לא הוזכר אלא בישראל גבי אסא דכתיב עם ערים בצורות אשר ביהודה כדאי' בקדושין דף כ"ז ואפ"ה פשיטא ליה לתשובת א"ש הנ"ל דמהני בגוי (ואף ע"ג דבקנין חליפין חולק הש"ך על ר"ת בח"מ סי' תך"ג וס"ל דלא מהני בגוי היינו משום דכתיב גבי חליפין וזאת לפנים בישראל) וא"כ בתורת חצר קונה לגוי אפי' שלא מדעתו וכמו שכתב בתשובת ע"ה הנ"ל אולם כ"ז לא יועיל ולא עלתה ארוכה לשבר בת עמי לעת כזאת אשר נודע ביהוד' ובגוי' שהמכירה היא רק להפקיע איסור חמץ אף החרדים עד"ה ומכרו בלב שלם מ"מ אין דעת הגוי לקנות המקום ולא החמץ ואם כן במה נקנה החמץ לגוי כיון דגם החצר אינה נקנה לו כיון דאין חפץ לקנות החצר כלל (וגם בתורת אגב בלבד מ"ש לעיל. ראיתי בס' או"ת סי' קך"ג דאגב אינו קונה בגוי ופשיט' ליה מלתא ולא הזכיר דברי תשו' א"ש הנ"ל ע"ש) ולבי א"ל דדוקא בימים הקדמונים שהיה דבר זה במכירת חמץ לגוי דרך מקרה. והיה המכירה בלב בין אצל ישראל המוכר ובין אצל הגוי הקונה אבל עתה בעו"ה הן רבים עתה ע"ה שגם בעיניהם הדבר רק מצות אנשים ומנהג אבותיהם בידיהם. כ"ש שאין דעת הגוי לקנות כלל בעניותי הדבר קשה בעיני הרבה ומה אעשה ולחלישות שכלי בעו"ה לא ידעתי לתקן אם שנסמוך על מ"ש הרב"י בשם הר"ן בסי' תל"א כיון דבלא"ה אין החמץ ברשותו כו' וכמ"ש מ"א בשם מ"ב אך אין זה מספיק לענ"ד אח"ז עיינתי בנימוקי יוסף אמתני' דראה את המציא' ונפל עליה ובא אחר והחזיק בה זה שהחזיק בה קנה דאמרינן שם ג"כ הטעם גלי' דעתיה דבנפילה ניחא ליה לקנות כו' וז"ל וזו (ר"ל קנין ד' אמות) כיון דתקנת חכמים היא. שומעים לו באומר א"א בתקנת חכמים כגון זו עכ"ל. משמע דהיכי דאיכא קנין מן התורה קונה אע"ג דלא ניחא ליה לקנות וכ"כ להדיא בס' שטה מקובצת אלא שכ' שהרשב"א חולק ואייתי ראיה מיבמות דכ"ב ע"ב מעורר בנכסי גר וסובר שהן שלו דלא קני והכי קיי"ל סי' רע"ה. מ"מ כבר יש יתד לתלות בו גם הביא בשם הרא"ה דלא קי"ל כהאי תירוצא דגליה דעתיה ע"ש בס' שטה מ':
וכ"ד שנהגו הסוחרים כו' ר"ל סוחרים ישראל והוא דין סטימתא המבואר בח"מ סי' ר"א אכן כתב שם הש"ך בשם הב"ח דבקרקע אין סטימת' קונה אלא אם כן נודע בבירור שהמנהג לקנות קרקע ע"י סטימתא במקום ההוא. וכ"ש הקנין שבין גוי לישראל דבדיניהם פשוט הוא כו' גם נתן מקצת דמים כו' דבתשובת ע"ה סי' ק"ב כתב וז"ל ועוד א"ל שגם בדיניהם לא יפסקו כן אלא במכירה גמורה אבל בנדון דידן שמכרו שתי פרות בעד חצי פ"ג אפשר שגם בדיניהם אינו קונה אע"פ שהתוס' כתבו בע"ז פ"ב דף ע"א אמנם א"צ שיתן הגוים מעות שוה כו' אלא סגי שיקנה בפרוטה עכ"ל. היינו דוקא כשאין אנו צריכים לדיניהם אבל כשאנו צריכים לדיניהם ונימוסיהם אפשר דבעי' דוקא שוה כל דמי שווי הבהמה ודבר זה צריך חקיר' גדולה בנימוסיהם עכ"ל:
מ"ש אזלינן כו' היינו בתשובת מ"ב הנ"ל:
וכ"מ ביורה דעה סי' ש"ך כו' מדהוצרכו הפוסקים למצוא תקנה למכור הבהמה להפקיע קדושת בכור ע"י כסף ומשיכה או הקנאת מקום כנ"ל טפי ה"ל לתקן בקל להקנות ע"י קנין דמהני בדיניהם. מזה אייתי ש"ך סי' קכ"ג ראיה דלא כר"ת דס"ל דמהני חליפין בגוי דא"כ ה"ל לפוסקים ליתן תיקון זה בחמץ ובכור להקנות ע"י חליפין א"ו דס"ל דל"מ חליפין בגוי ע"ש. דאמרינן אדעתיה דגוי אפקרא כו' הם דברי הש"ס ב"ק דף קט"ז ע"א רב ספרא הוי אזיל בשיירתא ונתחבר עמהם ארי לשמור בהמותם מחיות ולסטים והיו נותנים לו כל לילה חמור א' לאכול כי מטו זמנא דרב ספרא יהיב לו חמורו ולא אכלו בשחר קדם רב ספרא וזכי בחמורו א"ל ר"א מדפתא לרבינא ל"ל לר"ס למזכי ביה הא אדעתיה דארי' אפקרי' ולא אדעתיה דכ"ע א"ל לרווחא דמלתא זכי ביה. אולם בתשובת מ"ב לא הזכיר טעם זה אלא הביא ראיה מדין סקריקון והם הורגי נפשות אם אנסו לא' למכור להם קרקעו דהקנין קיים דאגב אונסי' גמר ומקני ומ"מ קי"ל אי קנה ישראל אחר מן הסקריקון צריך לחזור לבעלים הראשונים ובמקח הזול כדרך שלוקחים מן הסקריקו' ועוד הביא ראיה ממערופי' ואפי' במקומות שאין דנין דין מערופי' כמבואר בח"מ סי' קנ"ו סעיף ה' בהג"ה שניה. מ"מ הכא עדיפא ע"ש שהאריך. אך טעמו של המ"א לא הבנתי דהא בהפקר ק"ל בסי' רע"ג דצריך שיפקיר בין לעניים ובין לעשירים דהיינו שיפקירנו לכל העולם דאל"כ לא הוי הפקר כלל וה"ה לענין מכירה. ואפשר כוונתו כמ"ש הט"ז דרשאי להתנות עם הגוים בשעת המכירה דאינו רשאי למוכרו לאחר אלא יעכבנו לעצמו או ימכרנו שוב לו להמוכר ואז אין ישראל אחר רשאי לקנותה מן הגוי ואם קנה ישראל אחר מהגוי רשאי המוכר לתובעו בדין שאין מכירת הגוי מועלת דזכות זה שיירת' לעצמו שאינו רשאי למוכרו לישראל אחר וממילא בטל' מכירת הגוי לישראל אחר ע"ש והמ"א ס"ל דסתמא דמלתא הוי כאלו התנה כן. ובח"י מביא בשם תשוב' צ"צ דאפי' אי (לא) אזלי' בתר דיניה' וגם דבקנין דידוע דבדיניהם לא מהני מ"מ אם מצד אלמות הגוי א"א להוציא החמץ מתחת ידו מהני ע"ש:

[4] Se'if katan 4: Outside, etc. The explanation is that this also refers to the chametz. It sounds that the non-Jew himself must certainly be outside the house, and that it is forbidden to sell to a non-Jew who lives with him, and this is the view of the Beis Yosef. But the later authorities disagreed: Terumas HaDeshen's intent is only about the chametz, that it should be outside the house. Regarding the non-Jew, we do not care, unless he is his Canaanite slave, whose body is acquired by him, and in this matter the slave's hand is like the master's hand.
[4] And if he has much chametz and it is impossible for him to remove it, etc. This implies that specifically in such a case, where it is impossible to remove it, it is permitted. But if it is possible to remove it from the house, he must remove it. So too Eliyah Rabbah wrote, that this was the custom in Prague: beer sellers had to remove all the chametz from their houses. They asked him why they differed from liquor sellers, who were permitted to have the chametz in their houses and sell it to a non-Jew. He answered them that liquor sellers are different, because it is impossible for them to remove the chametz; see there.
[4] "But only with a document" means that we require both, money and a document. It makes no difference whether he gave the money first or the document first, as is there in Choshen Mishpat. Shlah wrote that even if the document was written in our script, meaning Jewish writing, it is effective. This is his language: he writes to the non-Jew, "I have sold such-and-such room with everything inside it." This is the end of his words. Regarding what he wrote, "with everything, etc.," see what I will write below.
[4] And he should stipulate, etc. With money alone. Shlah concluded about this: nevertheless, one must inform the non-Jew and explain the matter to him well, so that his mind rely on the leniencies. This is his language.
[4] Bach. In truth, here the Bach wrote that it is enough if he stipulates that the non-Jew acquire it with money alone. However, there in Choshen Mishpat, the Shach brought in the name of the Bach that he disagrees with this law and holds that it is ineffective to stipulate that it be acquired by money alone. Perhaps with chametz the Bach is lenient because in any case it is not in his domain, except that Scripture treated it as though it were in his domain, as Magen Avraham writes afterward.
[4] "And see siman 450, se'if 5" means that the Bach wrote: although it is possible to rent the room to the non-Jew, since rental of land is acquired by money alone even for a non-Jew, it is not possible for two reasons. First, we hold that rental does not acquire. Second, the Yerushalmi states that one may not rent a room to non-Jews to use for chametz. Pri Chadash rejected these reasons. Regarding what he wrote that rental does not acquire, nevertheless with chametz it is effective, as we say in Pesachim 4: chametz is different, for it is written, "it shall not be found," and through rental it is also not found with him. And regarding what he wrote that the Yerushalmi forbids, we do not hold like that Yerushalmi. Nevertheless, as a matter of law he agreed with the Bach that there is no remedy through rental, because he would be earning from items forbidden for benefit, which is forbidden. For this reason, in siman 450, se'if 5, Magen Avraham, se'if katan 6, he wrote that one may not rent to a non-Jew on the eve of Pesach or during Pesach for him to place chametz there. This is Magen Avraham's intent in referring to siman 450, se'if 5. From this it sounds that lending is permitted. So too Pri Chadash wrote there. Lending is also acquired by money alone, and through this he can also acquire chametz.
[4] "And see Shlah." I have already brought it above.
[4] And Mas'as Binyamin, etc. With money and pulling, etc. At the beginning of chapter HaZahav, R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree. R. Yochanan holds that biblically money acquires for a Jew, and Scripture wrote, "when you sell a sale to your fellow," excluding a non-Jew. If so, for a non-Jew acquisition by money is ineffective, and pulling is required. Reish Lakish holds that biblically, for a Jew, pulling acquires. If so, for a non-Jew it is the reverse: specifically money acquires, not pulling. Rashi and those in his school ruled like Reish Lakish, and Rabbeinu Tam and those in his school ruled like R. Yochanan. To satisfy both, in Yoreh De'ah, siman 320, regarding removing the sanctity of a firstborn by transferring the mother while pregnant to a non-Jew, since an animal belonging to a non-Jew is exempt from firstborn sanctity, he required for this acquisition both money and pulling, or transfer of the place where the animal stands, and through this he also acquires the cow. The same applies here.
[4] It should read: that most poskim hold like Rashi. In truth, the later authorities wrote that on the contrary, most poskim hold like Rabbeinu Tam. But there is no practical difference as a matter of law, because nevertheless after the fact money alone is effective. For Mas'as Binyamin wrote that even pulling alone is effective after the fact, even though in his view most poskim hold that with non-Jews specifically money is required. If so, the same applies in reverse according to us: after the fact, money alone is effective, even though most poskim hold like Rabbeinu Tam that with a non-Jew pulling is required. A disclosure of intent is enough, as written in Beis Yosef, siman 431, for this reason that nullification works as ownerless designation. According to several poskim, even nullification in the heart is effective, although such a thing would not help regarding ownerless designation, since he did not say the language of ownerless designation but only nullified it, making it like dust. Even according to the view that ownerless designation specifically requires three people. This is as written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 273, se'if 7.
[4] And this requires examination, for in the Yerushalmi, etc. It says that a non-Jew cannot make his fellow non-Jew an agent, etc. Regarding transferring the place, many were confused. In Sefer Chok Yaakov he wrote in the name of Responsa Even Shoham that the intent is not that by transferring the place it becomes the non-Jew's courtyard and his courtyard acquires the chametz for him, for courtyard is derived through agency, and there is no agency for a non-Jew. Rather, the intent must be by way of agav, that movable goods are acquired together with land. According to this, he must use the language of agav and not the language of "with," as written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 202, according to one view there. However, Responsa Avodas HaGershuni, end of siman 120, wrote that for this reason the Tur in Yoreh De'ah, siman 320, regarding removing the sanctity of a firstborn, wrote that the clearest of the acquisitions is that he transfer the place to him. In that responsum he gave the reason why this acquisition is the clearest: with pulling, the non-Jew's intent is only to acquire with money, and whenever the buyer does not intend to acquire, the acquisition is ineffective. He brought proof from Bava Metzia 10, where a poor person fell on pe'ah and they remove him from it, for he did not acquire it. Although we hold that a person's four cubits acquire for him, nevertheless, since he fell on it, he revealed that he wants to acquire by falling and not through his four cubits, and therefore the four cubits do not acquire for him. Thus the acquisition depends on the buyer's intent. So too wrote Beis Yosef in siman 134, and also the Bach there, and he wrote that Responsa Maharam Mintz wrote likewise and brought many proofs. Therefore transferring the place is preferable, because his courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge; this is the content of his words. According to this, he necessarily holds that the reason is that a courtyard acquires for a non-Jew, not because of agav. For if it were because of agav, we would still require the non-Jew's intent, and on the contrary, acquisition by agav is difficult to explain to a non-Jew, and it is unlikely that the non-Jew intends to acquire by agav. Rather, according to Responsa Avodas HaGershuni, the reason must be through the law of courtyard. But then the difficulty of Responsa Even Shoham mentioned above applies to him, for there is no agency for a non-Jew. I found that in Responsa Avodas HaGershuni, end of siman 105, he sensed this and wrote: one can also say, regarding how a non-Jew's courtyard acquires for him, since courtyard is based on agency and we hold there is no agency for a non-Jew, and I wrote at length about this in another responsum. This is his language. I did not find anything about this in his printed responsa that came into my hands. Perhaps one can say that he holds like the Mas'as Binyamin brought by Magen Avraham, that a non-Jew can become an agent for a non-Jew, since both are not members of the covenant. Only when the sender is a member of the covenant must the agent also be a member of the covenant, and the same in reverse: when the agent is a member of the covenant, the sender must also be a member of the covenant. But when both sender and agent are not members of the covenant, it is acceptable. According to this, even though courtyard is based on agency, nevertheless a courtyard acquires for a non-Jew, because the courtyard is also not a member of the covenant and can become an agent for a non-Jew. Responsa Even Shoham follows its own approach, for it was not clear to him whether a non-Jew can become an agent for a non-Jew, as written in Sefer Chok Yaakov in his name, and therefore he wrote not to transfer to a non-Jew by way of courtyard, but only by way of agav. If so, since Magen Avraham proved from the Yerushalmi that a non-Jew cannot become an agent for a non-Jew, then we hold like Responsa Even Shoham, that courtyard does not acquire for a non-Jew, and one must transfer the chametz to him by way of agav.
[4] I already wrote that it is difficult to transfer to a non-Jew by way of agav, because the non-Jew does not rely in his mind on acquiring by agav, and wherever he does not intend to acquire by this mode of acquisition, he does not acquire, as I wrote in the name of Responsa Avodas HaGershuni in the name of the poskim. Therefore it occurred to me that it is preferable to sell to a non-Jewish woman who has no husband. In such a case one can say that Responsa Even Shoham concedes that her courtyard acquires for her, for it is explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 243, that a minor boy has no courtyard, since for a man courtyard was included through agency, and there is no agency for a minor. But a minor girl has a courtyard, for regarding a woman courtyard was included through "hand," and a minor girl has a hand. If so, a non-Jewish woman should have a courtyard, since she has a hand. Although the fact that courtyard was included for a woman through hand is learned from a get, as stated at the beginning of Bava Metzia, and a get does not apply to a non-Jew, nevertheless one can say that since a non-Jew was not excluded from this acquisition, the law is the same with a non-Jewish woman. Know that acquisition by agav is mentioned only with regard to a Jew, in the case of Asa, as it is written, "with fortified cities that are in Yehudah," as stated in Kiddushin 27, and nevertheless Responsa Even Shoham took it as obvious that it is effective with a non-Jew. And although with exchange acquisition the Shach disagrees with Rabbeinu Tam in Choshen Mishpat, siman 423, and holds that it is ineffective with a non-Jew, that is because regarding exchange it is written, "and this formerly in Israel." If so, through the law of courtyard she acquires for a non-Jew even without her knowledge, as Responsa Avodas HaGershuni wrote. However, all this will not help and does not provide a cure for the fracture of my people at this time, when it is known among Jews and non-Jews that the sale is only to remove the prohibition of chametz. Even the God-fearing who tremble at the word of Hashem and sell wholeheartedly, nevertheless the non-Jew does not intend to acquire the place or the chametz. If so, through what is the chametz acquired by the non-Jew, since even the courtyard is not acquired by him, because he does not desire at all to acquire the courtyard? And even by way of agav alone, regarding what I wrote above, I saw in Sefer Urim VeTumim, siman 123, that agav does not acquire for a non-Jew, and he took the matter as obvious and did not mention the words of Responsa Even Shoham mentioned above; see there. My heart tells me that specifically in earlier days, when this matter of selling chametz to a non-Jew was occasional, and the sale was wholehearted both for the Jewish seller and for the non-Jewish buyer, it was effective. But now, because of our many sins, there are many ignoramuses for whom even in their own eyes the matter is only a rote commandment and an ancestral custom, all the more so that the non-Jew has no intention to acquire at all. In my poverty of understanding, the matter is very difficult in my eyes. What shall I do? Because of the weakness of my intellect, through our many sins, I do not know how to repair it, unless we rely on what Beis Yosef wrote in the name of Ran in siman 431, that since in any case the chametz is not in his domain, etc., and as Magen Avraham wrote in the name of Mas'as Binyamin. But in my humble opinion this is not sufficient. Afterward I examined Nimukei Yosef on the Mishnah, "one who saw a found object and fell upon it, and another came and took hold of it, the one who took hold of it acquired it," where they also say the reason: he revealed his view that he wants to acquire by falling, etc. This is his language: this, meaning the acquisition of four cubits, since it is a rabbinic enactment, we listen to him when he says, "I do not want this enactment of the sages," in a case like this. This is his language. This implies that where there is a biblical acquisition, he acquires even though he does not want to acquire. So too is written explicitly in Sefer Shitah Mekubetzes, except that he wrote that Rashba disagrees and brings proof from Yevamos 52b regarding one who fences the property of a convert thinking it is his own, that he does not acquire; and so we hold in siman 275. Nevertheless, there is already a peg on which to hang the matter. He also brought in the name of Ra'ah that we do not rule like that answer that he revealed his intent; see there in Shitah Mekubetzes.
[4] And any matter that merchants customarily use, etc. This means Jewish merchants, and it is the law of situmta explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 201. However, the Shach there wrote in the name of the Bach that with land, situmta does not acquire unless it is clearly known that the custom in that place is to acquire land by situmta. "And all the more so the acquisition between a non-Jew and a Jew, for in their laws it is simple, etc.; he also gave part of the money, etc." In Responsa Avodas HaGershuni, siman 102, he wrote: moreover, one can say that even in their laws they would not rule so except in a complete sale. But in our case, where they sold two cows for half a p/g, perhaps even in their laws he does not acquire, although Tosafos wrote in Avodah Zarah, chapter 2, page 71, that the non-Jew need not give money equal to the value, but it is enough that he acquire with a perutah. That is specifically where we do not need their laws. But where we need their laws and customs, perhaps we require specifically the full value of the animal. This matter requires great investigation in their laws. This is his language.
[4] What he wrote, that we follow, etc. This refers to the Responsa Mas'as Binyamin mentioned above.
[4] And so it appears in Yoreh De'ah, siman 320, etc. Since the poskim needed to find a remedy for selling the animal to remove the sanctity of a firstborn through money and pulling, or through transfer of place, as above, it would have been better for them to make the simple remedy of transferring it through an acquisition effective under their laws. From this the Shach in siman 123 brought proof against Rabbeinu Tam, who holds that exchange is effective with a non-Jew: if so, the poskim should have given this remedy for chametz and a firstborn, to transfer through exchange. Rather, it must be that they hold exchange is ineffective with a non-Jew; see there. "For we say he made it ownerless with the non-Jew in mind, etc." These are the words of the Talmud in Bava Kamma 116a: Rav Safra was traveling with a caravan, and a lion joined them to guard their animals from wild animals and bandits, and every night they would give it one donkey to eat. When Rav Safra's turn arrived, he gave it his donkey and it did not eat it. In the morning Rav Safra rose early and acquired his donkey. Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina: why did Rav Safra need to acquire it? He made it ownerless with the lion in mind, not with everyone in mind. He answered him: he acquired it only for extra measure. However, Responsa Mas'as Binyamin did not mention this reason, but brought proof from the law of sikrikon, murderers who coerced someone to sell them his land, where the acquisition stands because under coercion he resolved and transferred it; nevertheless, we hold that if another Jew bought it from the sikrikon, he must return it to the original owners, at the cheap price for which people buy from the sikrikon. He also brought proof from ma'arufya, and even in places where they do not judge by the law of ma'arufya, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 156, se'if 5, in the second gloss, nevertheless here it is stronger; see there, where he wrote at length. But I did not understand Magen Avraham's reason, for regarding ownerless designation we hold in siman 273 that one must make it ownerless both for the poor and for the rich, meaning that he must make it ownerless to the whole world, for otherwise it is not ownerless at all. The same should apply to sale. Perhaps his intent is as Taz wrote, that one may stipulate with the non-Jew at the time of sale that he is not permitted to sell it to another, but must either keep it for himself or sell it back to the seller. Then another Jew is not permitted to buy it from the non-Jew, and if another Jew did buy it from the non-Jew, the seller may sue him in court, because the non-Jew's sale is ineffective, since the seller reserved this right for himself that the non-Jew may not sell it to another Jew. Automatically the non-Jew's sale to the other Jew is void; see there. Magen Avraham holds that in an ordinary case it is as though he stipulated this. Chok Yaakov brings in the name of Responsa Tzemach Tzedek that even if we do not follow their laws, and even with an acquisition known to be ineffective under their laws, nevertheless if because of the non-Jew's forcefulness it is impossible to remove the chametz from his hand, it is effective; see there.

magen_avraham.he:
שמא אצטרך. והטור כ' שרשאי לומ' לו קח במאתים ואקחנו ממך אחר הפסח ע"ש:
ה"ז עובר בבל יראה. דהמפקיד חמצו ביד עכו"ם עובר כמ"ש ססי' ת"מ (מ"מ) וצ"ל דמיירי שהישראל תלה התנאי בעצמו כגון שהתנה שאם הישראל יהיה לו מעות יחזירם לו דכה"ג לא הוי מכירה כלל כמ"ש בח"מ סי' ר"ז ע"ש וגרע ממשכון דבמשכון א"ל אם לא אפדנו קודם ר"ח אייר יהיה שלך מעכשיו אבל הכא לעול' הרשו' בידו לפדותו א"נ שתלה הישראל המכירה בתנאי כגון שא"ל אם תעשה לי דבר פלוני החמץ שלך נמצא דכל זמן שלא נתקיים התנאי לא הוי מכירתו מכירה אבל אם אמר הריני נותן לך מעכשיו על מנת להחזיר או על מנת שתעשה דבר פלוני הרי זה מכירה גמורה כמ"ש בח"מ סימן רי"ב ס"ד ובא"ע סי' כ"ח ס"כ ע"ש רק משום חומרא דחמץ אסור כמש"ל בס"ג:
magen_avraham.en:
[4] Perhaps I will need it. The Tur wrote that he is permitted to say to him, "Buy it for two hundred, and I will buy it back from you after Pesach"; see there.
[4] He transgresses bal yera'eh. For one who deposits his chametz with a non-Jew transgresses, as written at the end of siman 440 (Maggid Mishneh). One must say that this refers to where the Jew made the condition depend on himself, such as where he stipulated that if the Jew has money he will return it to him; in such a case it is not a sale at all, as written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 207; see there. It is worse than a pledge, for with a pledge he says to him, "If I do not redeem it before Rosh Chodesh Iyyar, it shall be yours from now." But here the power to redeem it is always in his hand. Alternatively, the Jew made the sale depend on a condition, such as if he said to him, "If you do such-and-such for me, the chametz is yours." It follows that as long as the condition has not been fulfilled, his sale is not a sale. But if he said, "I hereby give it to you from now on condition that you return it," or "on condition that you do such-and-such," this is a complete sale, as written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 212, se'if 4, and in Even HaEzer, siman 28, se'if 20; see there. It is forbidden only because of the stringency of chametz, as I wrote above in se'if 3.

mishnah_berurah.he:
(כב) עד שאתה לוקח חמץ במנה וכו' - ר"ל שיקח חמץ הרבה בסך מאתים אע"פ שא"צ ליקח אלא במנה שכשאצטרך אחר הפסח אקחנו ממך ואתן לך ריוח על כל הסך:
(כג) שמא אצטרך וכו' - והאחרונים כתבו דרשאי אפילו להבטיח שיחזור ויקנה ממנו ויתן לו ריוח:
(כד) על תנאי - מיירי שאמר בלשון אם דהיינו אם תעשה דבר פלוני בתוך הפסח או לאחר הפסח החמץ נתון לך או מכור לך דכל זמן שלא נתקיים התנאי עדיין אין החמץ מכור ונתון ולפיכך עובר בבל יראה אבל אם אמר לו הריני נותן לך מעכשיו ע"מ שתעשה דבר פלוני שייך החמץ לעכו"ם תיכף אם יתקיים התנאי לבסוף ואינו אסור רק משום חומרא דחמץ וכדלעיל בסוף ס"ג א"נ מיירי אפילו במעכשיו רק התנאי היה שאימתי שיביא מעות יחזירם לו ובתנאי זה לא חל המכירה והמתנה כלל כיון שכל שעה הרשות בידו לפדותו וכמבואר בחו"מ סימן ר"ז ס"ו. ודע עוד דהסכימו אחרונים דה"ה שאסור לומר לעכו"ם אני מוכר לך החמץ ע"מ שתחזיקנו לעצמך ולא תמכור לאדם אחר חוץ ממני דכיון דבלשון תנאי הוא כשיעבור העכו"ם וימכרנו לאדם אחר תבטל המכירה למפרע ונמצא שלא היה החמץ קנוי לעכו"ם מעולם וחיישינן שמא ימכרנו ויעבור הישראל על בל יראה אבל אם אמר לו הריני מוכר לך מכירה גמורה לחלוטין וזכות זה שיירתי לי בו שאם תרצה למוכרו לא תמכרנו לשום אדם חוץ ממני י"א דזה מותר אפילו לכתחלה דאפילו אם יעבור העכו"ם וימכור לא תבטל המכירה בשביל זה כיון דלא אמר בלשון תנאי רק שמכירת העכו"ם תהיה בטלה:
mishnah_berurah.en:
[4] (22) Instead of your buying chametz for one hundred, etc. This means that he should buy a large amount of chametz for the sum of two hundred, even though he needs to buy only for one hundred, so that when I need it after Pesach I will buy it from you and give you profit on the entire sum.
[4] (23) Perhaps I will need, etc. The later authorities wrote that he is permitted even to promise that he will go back and buy it from him and give him profit.
[4] (24) On condition. This refers to where he said it in the language of "if," meaning: if you do such-and-such during Pesach or after Pesach, the chametz is given to you or sold to you. As long as the condition has not been fulfilled, the chametz is not yet sold or given, and therefore he transgresses bal yera'eh. But if he said to him, "I hereby give it to you from now, on condition that you do such-and-such," the chametz belongs to the non-Jew immediately if the condition is ultimately fulfilled, and it is forbidden only because of the stringency of chametz, as above at the end of se'if 3. Alternatively, it refers even to a case of "from now," but the condition was that whenever he brings money, he must return it to him. With this condition, the sale or gift does not take effect at all, since at every moment it is in his power to redeem it, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 207, se'if 6. Know further that the later authorities agreed that the same applies: it is forbidden to say to a non-Jew, "I sell you the chametz on condition that you keep it for yourself and not sell it to anyone else except me." Since this is in the language of condition, if the non-Jew violates it and sells it to someone else, the sale is void retroactively, and it emerges that the chametz was never acquired by the non-Jew; we are concerned that he may sell it, and the Jew will transgress bal yera'eh. But if he said to him, "I hereby sell it to you as a complete absolute sale, and I have reserved this right in it, that if you want to sell it, you shall not sell it to anyone except me," some say this is permitted even ab initio. For even if the non-Jew violates this and sells it, the sale will not be void because of this, since he did not say it in the language of condition; only the non-Jew's sale will be void.

peri_megadim.he:
לעכו״ם עט״ז וצ״ל דלא מהני אלא שמחוץ לבית. ודיעבד אף בלא ייחד זוית כל שלא קיבל אחריות שרי ולכתחלה כתבו ז״ל שראוי למכור החדר ג״כ עמ״א ד׳ ואי״ה שם יבואר עא״י אות י״ג בשם ש״א סימן ג׳ דאין למכור חמץ לעבד כנעני שלו ועא״ר אות ו׳.והנה אף אין אחרים מוכרים לו ועי״ד סי׳ רס״ז סי״ז בלא טבל אין גופו קנוי לו אפ״ה מעשה ידיו וכל שיש לו לרבו ולא נ״מ אלא אם טבל שיצא לחירות ועש״ך אות למ״ד. ובטבל פשיטא דעבר בב״י בעשה ואפשר אף בעשה תשביתו עד הלילה ובמקום אחר כתבנו מזה ואם א׳ אמר לעבד וש״כ הריני נותן לך במתנה ע״מ להחזיר אחר הפסח לפי מ״ש הא״ר אות י״ח וכ״מ בלבוש דמתנה ע״מ להחזיר לכתחלה אסור משום חומרא דחמץ ודיעבד שרי בהנאה לאחר הפסח וכדבעינן למימר לקמן אי״ה אות ו׳ ומ״א ה׳ י״ל דהאדון לא קנה דלש״כ נמי לא הקנה ממש רק ע״מ שתחזיר לו ודומה לי״ד רס״ו סכ״ב ובש״ך אות ל״ט. וצ״ע:
ומ״ש הט״ז שאין להסגיר החדר כו׳ עח״י אות י״ד וא״ר ז׳ דוקא קודם המכירה הא מכר כדין וקנה עכו״ם ואח״כ הניח אותם אע״פ שאין ראוי וגוערין בו מ״מ דיעבד שרי:
ומעשה בא׳ שמכר חביות גדולות יי״ש והניח חותם לאחר המכירה יש להתיר ואף קודם המכירה מכירה דידן בשטר כראוי כל קוואר״ט בסך כך וכך והעכו״ם אם רוצה פותח אותם ועושה מה שרוצה רק החותם עד למדידה א״כ שרי ואפשר אף לכתחלה והנה בח״י כתב מטעם הערמה ועב״ח וזה במכירה מועטת דהוי ביטול מקח רק בגילוי דעת סגי כר״ן ר״פ וכל שהניח חותם קודם נראה שאין רוצה במכירה משא״כ כה״ג כאמור. וגם מ״ש הב״ח שלא יניח חותם על החדר הא על החביות יוכל העכו״ם למכור לחבירו החביות במשיכה וימדוד אחר הפסח ועא״ר דעכו״ם לא סמכה דעתיה משא״כ מכירה שלנו הראוי ולא הוי גילוי דעת ודאי דיעבד שרי ואף לכתחלה כה״ג דהחותם רק עד למדידה וזוקף עליו במלוה והיי״ש שלו מעתה ודע אם מוכר כל קווארט בסך רב י״ל דהוי ביטול מקח בעכו״ם ובזה ל״ש גילוי מלתא וראוי למכור כדרך העולם דליהוי מכירה כראוי וכ״ש אם היהודי מכר בכפר לעכו״ם היי״ש שיש לו בעיר והניח חותם ולא ידע העכו״ם מזה עדיף טפי דל״ש לא סמכה דעתו אלא אפי׳ שידע כה״ג דיעבד ודאי שרי. ומצאתי בכתבי א״א הרב ז״ל שו״ת א׳ מרבינו הגדול הגאון המפורסם בדורו הכהן הגדול מאחיו מהור״ר חיים כהן ראפפורט ז״ל אב״ד דק״ק לבוב והגליל הביא מ״ש המ״א אות ד׳ דמשמע מ״מ בדיעבד לא מסר המפתח שרי ואי״ה שם יבואר עוד:
ומ״ש שאין למכור החמץ למומר וחמץ של מומר אסור לכל ישראל ער״ן וכ״מ פ״א מחו״מ ה״ד וחולין ד׳ חמצן כו׳ ועח״י אות י״ד דאין ליקח אחר הפסח מיד חמץ מן מומר ואפשר ספק שמא נעשה אחר הפסח שרי עח״י תמ״ט א׳ וחולין ד׳ ב׳ ד״ה מותר ומהרש״א שם וא״ל דקושטא קאמר אף בדרבנן לא שביק היתרא דא״כ להכעיס נמי יהא שרי ובס׳ ראש יוסף כתבנו שם. ומיהו יש לומר לעשות לכתחלה ס״ס או ספק דרבנן אין עושין עי״ד ק״י וקכ״נ דקונים דברים מבושלים מעכו״ם דסתם אב״י וס״ס התם מדוחק הוא:
והוי יודע מומר שנשא עכו״ם הוולד עכו״ם ולהיפך הוולד ישראל עיין אה״ע מזה ומ״מ דיעבד צ״ע די״ל עדיף מתינוק שנשבה לבין עכו״ם ואין לך אונס גדול מזה ואף בישראל אנוס אסור זה עדיף טפי ודיעבד אם קנה ממנו בה״מ י״ל. ולמכור לאשת מומר לעכו״ם לכתחלה לא ואם א״א שאין אחר מוכר לה בתנאי שתחזיק לעצמך ולא תמכור אף לבעלך וכמ״ש הט״ז אות ו׳ בזה שרי:
ומה שכתב ומעשה כו׳ בסימן תמ״ג בט״ז ומ״א ה׳ ו׳ חליפי חמץ לאחרים מותר ומכל מקום דווקא בהפסד מרובה הא הפסד מועט אין להשיאו עצה בכך. וגם שמא ימכור עכו״ם לישראל. ועיין משנה למלך פרק ה׳ מהלכות אישות הלכה א׳ סוף ד״ה הכלל העולה שלא מצא מבואר אם איסורי הנאה דרבנן אסור למחליף עצמו יע״ש. וברש״י חולין ד׳ ב׳ מבואר דרבנן ג״כ אסור למחליף עצמו. וכי תימא שפירש כן לסלקא דעתך דר׳ יהודה א״כ מרויחין דהוה דרבנן ובתוספות ד״ה מותר י״ל כן ובספר ראש יוסף הארכתי שם.
אם קנו חמץ שעבר הפסח מן מומר ולא ידע שהוא מומר וכדומה פשיטא דמקח טעות הוא עיין משנה למלך פרק ה׳ מהלכות אישות הלכה ז׳ (במשנה למלך) ובהלכות מכירה פרק י״ו הלכה י״ד וביורה דעה קי״ט סעיף י״ג ואם ירצה המומר להחזיר המעות רשאי דשלו הוא נוטל וכאמור. עיין ביורה דעה בסימן צ״ט בש״ך אות י״ז כתבתי בשם גאון אחד מעשה באחד שלקח מיד לאחר הפסח דוודאי נעשה בפסח רק שחבית אחת נעשה אחר הפסח י״ל דמותר להוסיף ולבטלו יע״ש. הנה בלא הפסד מרובה אין להתיר דיש ספק ספיקא לאיסורא שמא הלכה כהר״ב דאין מוסיפין בדרבנן ושמא הכל נעשה בתוך הפסח. וכל שכן אם עירב הכל ביחד נעשית נבילה לח בלא בישול עיין יורה דעה צ״ט. אבל בהפסד מרובה י״ל אף רובא דאיסורא ומיעוט היתר כההיא דעצים שנשרו לתוך ״התנור״ יבש ביבש שמע מינה רובא דאיסורא מוסיף ומבטל בדרבנן ושם ביארתיו. וחביות בין חביות גדולות דבר חשוב עיין יורה דעה (קל״ב) סעיף ב׳ אף בדרבנן לא בטל ועיין ט״ז תמ״ז אות י״ח תקנתיה דידיה. מעשה באחד שמכר חמץ ויין שרף לעכו״ם כראוי וזקף הדמים במלוה ובתוך הפסח הפסיד העכו״ם הרבה מיין שרף ולקח עכו״ם אוהבו של ישראל המפתח מיד העכו״ם לית חששא. ואפשר רשאי הישראל לקבול לפני השר שיקח המפתח מיד העכו״ם שלא יפסיד לגמרי כי הוא עכו״ם עני. אבל אם לקח הישראל המפתח מהעכו״ם י״ל דאחריות על ישראל ואסור לאחר הפסח וצ״ע. אפר חמץ שעבר הפסח צ״ע דאע״ג דכי קניס ר׳ שמעון בעיניה על ידי תערובת אף פחות מששים אפשר לא קניס כבסימן תמ״ז במ״א מ״ד אפר אפשר גרע טפי. ואם שהה חמץ על מנת לבערו בפסח ושרפו בפסח עיין תוספות פסחים כ״ט ב׳ ד״ה רב אשי י״ל דאפרו מותר דלא עבר בל יראה. ובפתיחה בריש הספר חלק א׳ פרק א׳ סעיף י״ב הארכתי. אבל קנה בפסח על מנת לבערו ובערו בהא לא קאמינא. ועיין משנה למלך בהלכות חמץ ומצה פרק א׳ (ופרק) ג׳:
peri_megadim.en:
[4] To a non-Jew. See Taz. One must say that it is effective only when it is outside the house. After the fact, even if he did not designate a corner, as long as he did not accept responsibility, it is permitted. Ab initio, the authorities wrote that it is proper also to sell the room; see Magen Avraham 4, where, with Hashem's help, this will be explained. See Eshel Avraham, note 13, in the name of Sha'ar Ephraim, siman 3, that one may not sell chametz to his Canaanite slave, and see Eliyah Rabbah, note 6. Even if others do not sell to him, see Yoreh De'ah, siman 267, se'if 17, that without immersion his body is not acquired by him. Even so, his handiwork and whatever he has belongs to his master, and there is a practical difference only if he immersed, for then he goes free; see Shach, note 30. If he immersed, it is obvious that his master transgresses bal yera'eh regarding the positive commandment, and perhaps even the positive commandment of tashbisu until nightfall; elsewhere we wrote about this. If someone said to a slave or maidservant, "I hereby give it to you as a gift on condition that you return it after Pesach," according to what Eliyah Rabbah wrote in note 18, and so it appears in Levush, that a gift on condition to return is forbidden ab initio because of the stringency of chametz but after the fact is permitted for benefit after Pesach, as we will say below, with Hashem's help, in note 6 and Magen Avraham 5, one can say that the master did not acquire it. For he also did not transfer it to the maidservant absolutely, but only on condition that she return it to him. This resembles Yoreh De'ah 266:22 and Shach, note 39. This requires examination.
[4] And what Taz wrote, that one should not lock the room, etc.: see Chok Yaakov, note 14, and Eliyah Rabbah 7. This applies specifically before the sale. But if he sold according to law and the non-Jew acquired it, and afterward he placed them there, although this is improper and we rebuke him, nevertheless after the fact it is permitted.
[4] And there was an incident involving one who sold large barrels of liquor and placed a seal after the sale; one may permit it. Even before the sale, regarding our sale that is done properly by document, with each quart for such-and-such amount, and the non-Jew may open them if he wishes and do what he wants, while the seal is only until measurement, it is permitted, and perhaps even ab initio. Chok Yaakov wrote the reason as evasion; see Bach. That is with a small sale, where it is a void sale and only a disclosure of intent is enough, as Ran wrote at the beginning of Pesachim. Whenever he placed the seal beforehand, it appears that he does not want the sale. But in a case like this, as stated, this is not so. Also, what the Bach wrote that one should not place a seal on the room implies that on the barrels he may, for the non-Jew can sell the barrels to his fellow by pulling, and they can be measured after Pesach. See Eliyah Rabbah, that the non-Jew does not rely on the transaction. But in our sale, which is proper and is not a disclosure of intent, it is certainly permitted after the fact, and even ab initio in such a case, where the seal is only until measurement and he records the debt as a loan, while the liquor is his from now. Know that if one sells each quart for a very large sum, one can say that this is a void sale with a non-Jew, and in this case the principle of mere disclosure does not apply. It is proper to sell in the ordinary way so that it be a proper sale. All the more so if the Jew sold to a non-Jew in a village the liquor that he had in the city, and he left a seal, and the non-Jew did not know of this, it is better, for the issue that the non-Jew does not rely on it does not apply. Even if he knew, in such a case it is certainly permitted after the fact. I found in the writings of my father and teacher, the Rav, of blessed memory, one responsum from our great teacher, the famous gaon in his generation, the great kohen from among his brothers, R. Chaim Kohen Rapoport, of blessed memory, Av Beis Din of the holy community of Lvov and the region. He brought what Magen Avraham wrote in note 4, implying that nevertheless after the fact, if he did not hand over the key, it is permitted, and with Hashem's help this will be explained further there.
[4] And what he wrote, that one may not sell the chametz to an apostate, and the chametz of an apostate is forbidden to every Jew: see Ran, and so it appears in chapter 1 of Hilchos Chametz U'Matzah, halachah 4, and Chullin 4, "their chametz, etc." See Chok Yaakov, note 14, that one should not buy chametz from an apostate immediately after Pesach. Perhaps a doubt that it may have been made after Pesach is permitted; see Chok Yaakov 449:1, Chullin 4b, s.v. "permitted," and Maharsha there. One cannot say that he is telling the truth, for even in rabbinic law one who transgresses for appetite does not leave permitted food and eat forbidden food, for if so, even one who transgresses spitefully should be permitted. We wrote about this there in Sefer Rosh Yosef. However, one can say that we do not create a double doubt ab initio, or even a rabbinic doubt; see Yoreh De'ah 110. It is somewhat comparable to buying cooked items from non-Jews where the default is that the utensil was not used that day and there is a double doubt, but there it is only under pressure.
[4] Know that if an apostate married a non-Jewish woman, the child is a non-Jew; and in the reverse case, the child is a Jew. See Even HaEzer regarding this. Nevertheless, after the fact it requires examination, for one can say that this is better than a child captured among non-Jews, and there is no greater unavoidable circumstance than this. Even with a Jew under duress the chametz is forbidden, but this case is better. After the fact, if one bought from him in a case of great loss, there is room to say. To sell to the apostate's non-Jewish wife ab initio, no. But if it is impossible and there is no one else, one may sell to her on condition that she keep it for herself and not sell it even to her husband, and as Taz wrote in note 6, this is permitted.
[4] What he wrote, "and there was an incident, etc.," is in siman 443 in Taz, and in Magen Avraham 5 and 6. Exchanges of chametz are permitted to others after Pesach. Nevertheless, this is specifically in a case of great loss; if there is only a small loss, one should not give him advice to do this. There is also concern that the non-Jew may sell it to a Jew. See Mishneh LeMelech, chapter 5 of Hilchos Ishus, halachah 1, at the end of s.v. "the general rule that emerges," where he did not find explicit whether items forbidden for benefit rabbinically are forbidden to the exchanger himself; see there. In Rashi, Chullin 4b, it is explicit that rabbinic prohibitions too are forbidden to the exchanger himself. If you will say that he explained so only according to the initial assumption of R. Yehudah, then they profit from it, which would be rabbinic; and in Tosafos, s.v. "permitted," one can say so. I wrote about this at length there in Sefer Rosh Yosef.
[4] If they bought chametz that remained over Pesach from an apostate and did not know that he was an apostate, or the like, it is obvious that this is a mistaken purchase. See Mishneh LeMelech, chapter 5 of Hilchos Ishus, halachah 7, and in Hilchos Mechirah, chapter 16, halachah 14, and Yoreh De'ah 119:13. If the apostate wants to return the money, he is permitted, for he is taking what is his, as stated. See Yoreh De'ah, siman 99, in Shach, note 17, where I wrote in the name of one gaon about an incident with one who bought immediately after Pesach what was certainly made on Pesach, except that one barrel was made after Pesach. One can say that it is permitted to add and nullify it; see there. Without great loss, one should not permit this, for there is a double doubt toward prohibition: perhaps the halachah follows Rema that one may not add to nullify even a rabbinic prohibition, and perhaps everything was made during Pesach. All the more so if he mixed everything together, it becomes forbidden like a neveilah, liquid without cooking; see Yoreh De'ah 99. But in a case of great loss, one can say that even a majority of prohibition with a minority of permitted matter is like the case of wood that fell into an oven, dry with dry, which shows that a majority of prohibition can have permitted matter added to nullify it in a rabbinic case; I explained it there. Barrels among large barrels are an important item; see Yoreh De'ah 132:2, that even rabbinically it is not nullified, and see Taz 447, note 18, regarding its remedy. There was an incident involving one who sold chametz and liquor to a non-Jew properly, and recorded the money as a loan. During Pesach, the non-Jew ruined much of the liquor, and a non-Jew who was friendly with the Jew took the key from the non-Jew; there is no concern. Perhaps the Jew may complain before the official so that he take the key from the non-Jew, lest he destroy everything, because he is a poor non-Jew. But if the Jew took the key from the non-Jew, one can say that responsibility rests on the Jew and it is forbidden after Pesach; this requires examination. The ash of chametz that remained over Pesach requires examination. Although when R. Shimon penalized, he penalized the substance itself, and perhaps not a mixture even in less than sixty, as in siman 447 in Magen Avraham 44, ash may be worse. If one kept chametz in order to destroy it on Pesach and burned it on Pesach, see Tosafos, Pesachim 29b, s.v. "Rav Ashi"; one can say that its ash is permitted, for he did not transgress bal yera'eh. In the introduction at the beginning of the book, part 1, chapter 1, se'if 12, I wrote at length. But if he acquired it on Pesach in order to destroy it and destroyed it, I am not saying this. See Mishneh LeMelech in Hilchos Chametz U'Matzah, chapter 1 and chapter 3.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: <small>מג"א ס"ק ד </small>אבל עכו"ם לעכו"ם עושה שליח וכ"כ הריק"ש חוה"מ סי' קפ"ח אבל מדברי בעה"ת הובאו בב"י יו"ד סי' קס"ט ובהגהות שם סי"א מוכח דנכרי לנכרי אין נעשה שליח כמ"ש התפל"מ שם וע' בב"ש אה"ע ססי' ה' ובשו"ת מהר"ם מינץ סי' ה' כתב אבל גוי לגוי אפשר דהוי שליח:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [4] <small>Magen Avraham, se'if katan 4.</small> "But a non-Jew can make another non-Jew an agent." So too wrote Rikash, Choshen Mishpat, siman 188. But from the words of Baal HaTerumos, brought in Beis Yosef, Yoreh De'ah, siman 169, and in the glosses there, se'if 11, it is proven that one non-Jew does not become an agent for another non-Jew, as Tefillah LeMoshe wrote there. See Beis Shmuel, Even HaEzer, end of siman 5. In Responsa Maharam Mintz, siman 5, he wrote: but perhaps a non-Jew can be an agent for a non-Jew.

turei_zahav.he: לעכו"ם שמחוץ לבית. ב"כ ב"י דמשמע מדברי ת"ה דלא מהני נתינת חמץ לעכו"ם (אא"כ הוא עכו"ם) שמחוץ לבית ואין הכוונ' שהעכו"ם יהי' איש נכרי ואין דר בבית ישראל אבל על החמץ אם הוא בבית ישראל אין קפידא דבר זה ודאי אין לו טעם וריח דגרע טפי מה שהחמץ בביתו ותו דבת"ה לא כ' שמחוץ לבית אלא מחוץ לבי' משמע דעל החמץ אמר שיהי' חוץ לבית ובעכו"ם לא איכפת לן אפי' אם הוא בבי' משר' שלו שהרי בסמוך מתיר אפי' מכי' אותו ורגיל בו ויודע כו' כ"ז כתבתי לדע' ב"י בשם ת"ה אבל עיקרא דמלתא לא נלע"ד דהא אית' בהדיא פ"ק ד"ז הבאתיו בסי' תע"ה דייחד לו קרן זוית לחמצו של עכו"ם אינו זקוק לבער דעכו"ם כי מעייל לדנפשיה קא מעייל משום שנא' לא ימצא בבתיכם יצא זה שאינו מצוי בידך ופירש"י שהרי אותו זוית מסורה לעכו"ם וש"מ דאפי' בבית מהני בייחד לו קרן זוית אלא ודאי דגם ת"ה לא בא למעט יחד לו קרן זוית דזה קרוי נמי חוץ לבית ישראל כנלע"ד פשוט: ופשוט הוא שהחמץ יהיה מונח במקום שהעכו"ם יכול לכנוס שם מעצמו כדמשמע לישנא דגמ' דעכו"ם עייל לדנפשיה וכ"ש שלא יסגירנו במסגרת וישראל יחזיק המפתח בידו או יניח חותמו עליו וגם צריך שימכו' לו בפי' אותו החדר עם החמץ שבו דאל"כ הרי הוא בבתיכם וכל שאינו עושה בדרך שזכרנו ה"ז עובר בב"י ובב"י וחמצו לאחר הפסח אסור בהנאה: ודבר פשוט הוא שאין למכור החמץ למומר דאע"פ שחטא ישראל הוא: ומעשה היה בא' מחזיק אורנד"א בכפר שמכר יין שרף שלו להפקיד שלו שהי' מומר והיה סך הרבה וקשה הדבר להפסיד היין שרף וקרוב היה שלא יציית ישראל בזה ואמרתי שיחליפנו הפקיד עם עכו"ם אחר ויקח ממנו יי"ש אחר ואז מותר לישראל זה כמו דאי' פ"ק דחולין חמץ של עוברי עבירה מותר אחר הפסח מפני שהן מחליפים פי' וחמץ אינו תופס דמיו וה"ה נמי אם ימכרנו הפקיד להעכו"ם מותרים המעות לישראל מטעם זה כנלע"ד:
turei_zahav.en: [4] To a non-Jew outside the house. The Beis Yosef wrote that it sounds from the words of Terumas HaDeshen that giving chametz to a non-Jew is ineffective unless he is a non-Jew outside the house. The intent is not that the non-Jew must be a foreign man who does not live in the Jew's house, while there is no concern if the chametz is in the Jew's house. That certainly has neither reason nor sense, for it is worse when the chametz is in his house. Furthermore, Terumas HaDeshen did not write "outside the house" regarding the non-Jew, but "outside the house" meaning that he said the chametz should be outside the house. As for the non-Jew, we do not care even if he is his household servant, for immediately afterward he permits it even where he recognizes him and is used to him, and knows, etc. All this I wrote according to the Beis Yosef's understanding in the name of Terumas HaDeshen. But the main point does not appear to me, for it is stated explicitly in the first chapter of Pesachim, which I brought in siman 475, that if he designated a corner for a non-Jew's chametz, he is not required to destroy it, because when the non-Jew brings it in, he brings it in for himself, as it says, "it shall not be found in your houses," excluding this, which is not in your control. Rashi explained: for that corner is given over to the non-Jew. We learn from here that even in the house it helps if he designates a corner for him. Rather, Terumas HaDeshen also certainly did not come to exclude designating a corner, for this too is called outside the Jew's house. This appears simple to me. And it is obvious that the chametz must be placed in a location where the non-Jew can enter on his own, as is implied by the language of the Gemara, that the non-Jew enters for himself. All the more so one should not lock it with a lock while the Jew keeps the key in his hand or places his seal on it. He must also explicitly sell him that room together with the chametz inside it, for otherwise it is still "in your houses." Anyone who does not act in the manner we mentioned transgresses bal yera'eh and bal yimatzei, and his chametz after Pesach is forbidden for benefit. It is also obvious that one must not sell the chametz to an apostate, for even though he sinned, he is a Jew. There was an incident involving one who held an arenda in a village and sold his liquor to his official, who was an apostate. The amount was large, and it was difficult to lose the liquor, and it was likely that the Jew would not obey in this matter. I said that the official should exchange it with another non-Jew and take other liquor from him, and then it is permitted to this Jew, as stated in the first chapter of Chullin: the chametz of transgressors is permitted after Pesach because they exchange it. This means that chametz does not render its proceeds forbidden. The same applies if the official sells it to a non-Jew: the money is permitted to the Jew for this reason, as appears to me.

mechaber.he: חמץ שנמצא בבית ישראל אחר הפסח אסור אע"פ שביטלו:
mechaber.en: Chametz that is found in a Jew's house after Passover is forbidden, even though he nullified it.

baer_heitev.he: שביטלו. אע"ג דלא עבר מן התורה מ"מ חיישינן שיערים לו' שביטלו אע"פ שלא ביטלו כיון שעשה שלא כתחז"ל שלא ביער החמץ או מכר לעכו"ם. ואפי' הפקר גמור גם כן דינא הכי ואפי' איכא עדים שהפקירו ובטלו לא מהני אם הניח חמץ בביתו וברשותו מדעתו וידע ממנו כל ימי פסח ודאי כה"ג לא מהני ביטול או הפקר אבל כל שלא היה יודע ממנו כל ימי פסח ויש עדים שביטל או הפקיר ק"פ או שיש אונס גמור בענין המכירה וכל ימי הפסח היה סבור שמכר ואחר הפסח נודע לו שלא מכר כיון שהיה אנוס כ"כ אונס ידוע ואמר שביטל אף דליכא עדים לא חיישינן להערמה ויש להתיר עכ"פ בהנאה אחר פסח. ח"י ע"ש. כתב הר"ש הלוי חא"ח סי' י"ב דאם נתעכב ליהודי חמץ על הדרך שהוא בספינ' היה נראה להתיר להפקיר כל חמצו ולחזור ולזכות בו אחר פסח ולמוכרו אבל לא לאוכלו ומפני חומרא דחמץ לא מלאני לבי לעשות מעשה עיין כנה"ג. וכתב המ"א ופשוט אפי' אין החמץ אצלו יכול למכור לעכו"ם החמץ באחד מדרכי הקנין הנ"ל ואז קנה העכו"ם החמץ בכ"מ שהוא ע"ש. ע' שו"ת עה"ג ס"ק ה' ועח"י:
baer_heitev.en: [5] That he nullified it. Even though he did not transgress biblically, nevertheless we are concerned that he will act evasively and say that he nullified it even though he did not nullify it, since he acted contrary to the sages' enactment by not destroying the chametz or selling it to a non-Jew. Even with complete ownerless designation, the law is also so. And even if there are witnesses that he made it ownerless and nullified it, this does not help if he intentionally left chametz in his house and domain and knew about it throughout all the days of Pesach; certainly in such a case nullification or ownerless designation does not help.
